item.title: Julia Salazar to hold ‘State Budget 101’ town hall in Bushwick on October 1
item.dc:creator: Bushwick Daily News Desk
item.description: State Senator Julia Salazar will hold a "State Budget 101" town hall on October 1 from 6 to 8 p.m. at 223 Linden St. in Bushwick.
item.content:encoded:
State Senator Julia Salazar will hold a “State Budget 101” town hall on Thursday, Oct. 1, from 6 to 8 p.m. at 223 Linden St. in Bushwick, where she will explain how New York’s budget is made and answer residents’ questions.

The town hall will cover how to get involved in the budget process, what the budget pays for, from roads and hospitals to raising or lowering income taxes, and the policy it carries beyond spending, including immigration, criminal justice, climate and housing. RSVP at nysenate.gov/StateBudget101.

“Want to know why it’s so complicated to tax the rich? Or why some projects in your community get funded, but others don’t?” Salazar wrote in her invitation. “And, did you know our State Budget does more than provide funding and dictate our state taxes? It also includes immigration protections, tenant protections, criminal justice reforms, and more.”

Questions about the event can go to Salazar’s office at (718) 573-1726 or teamsalazar@nysenate.gov. The invitation is in English and Spanish.

Salazar represents State Senate District 18, which covers North and East Brooklyn and Ridgewood, Queens. First elected in 2018, she has focused on tenant rights, affordable housing and rent regulation.

Featured image: Bushwick Daily archive

item.title: Bushwick housing lottery opens two one-bedrooms at 1052 Willoughby Avenue for $2,139 a month
item.dc:creator: Bushwick Daily News Desk
item.description: Households of one to three people earning $78,960 to $122,160 can apply through NYC Housing Connect until Thursday, Oct. 1.
item.content:encoded:
Two one-bedroom apartments at 1052 Willoughby Avenue in Bushwick are available through an NYC Housing Connect lottery at $2,139 a month, and applications close Thursday, October 1.

The apartments are set aside for households earning 80 percent of the area median income. A one-person household must earn $78,960 to $95,040 a year, a two-person household $78,960 to $108,560 and a three-person household $78,960 to $122,160, according to the listing. Households of one to three people can apply. The listing notes that the minimum income may not apply to applicants with Section 8 vouchers or other rental subsidies.

Applications are submitted online through NYC Housing Connect, the city’s affordable-housing portal, and there are no deposits or application fees, according to the listing.

The apartments have hardwood floors, split-system heating and air conditioning, an intercom entry system and security cameras, and some third-floor units have private patios or balconies, the listing says. One small pet up to 50 pounds is allowed per apartment, with a refundable $300 pet deposit that may be required. Tenants pay for electricity, which covers the electric heat and stove; hot water is included in the rent.

The building has eight apartments, and two are being offered in the lottery. It is expected to receive a property tax exemption through the city’s 485-x incentive program, according to the listing. Applicants’ assets are capped at $135,680, according to the listing.

The J, M and Z trains stop at Myrtle Avenue and nearby stations, the L at DeKalb Avenue, Jefferson Street and Morgan Avenue, and the G at Myrtle-Willoughby Avenues, according to the listing.

Another Brooklyn lottery is open on Housing Connect: 815 Kings Highway, which closes October 13.

Featured image: Image via NYC Housing Connect

item.title: New York City wins $131.5 million settlement from DoorDash for delivery workers
item.dc:creator: Bushwick Daily News Desk
item.description: Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration announced a $131.5 million settlement against DoorDash for violating New York City's Delivery Worker Laws, directing over $115 million to more than 260,000 underpaid delivery workers.
item.content:encoded:
Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani’s administration announced on September 22 a $131.5 million enforcement settlement against DoorDash over what it described as systematic violations of New York City’s Delivery Worker Laws, an action that will send money to more than 260,000 delivery workers the city says the company underpaid, paid late or never paid at all.

The settlement directs more than $115 million to workers and more than $16 million in civil penalties and costs, according to the Mayor’s Office. The office called it the largest worker settlement in New York City history and the largest settlement involving food delivery workers in the United States. Details are posted at nyc.gov/doordash, and the administration’s full announcement is on the city’s site.

Workers do not need to file a claim or submit evidence to be paid, the Mayor’s Office said. The Department of Consumer and Worker Protection identified everyone owed money by analyzing DoorDash’s own records. In late October, the agency’s settlement administrator will email each worker who experienced an underpayment between April 22, 2022 and June 28, 2026, sent to the last email address the worker used with DoorDash and stating the amount owed. Workers can choose an electronic payment or a check by mail; those who do not choose will be mailed a check to their last-known address. Payments begin this fall.

Compensation is calculated at roughly 200 percent of what a worker was underpaid. A worker owed $1,000 who received nothing will get $3,000, the office said, and a worker paid $1,000 later than the law allows will get $2,000.

The Department of Consumer and Worker Protection said its citywide investigation began after dozens of workers reported that DoorDash had failed to pay them, or paid them late, for work they had already performed. Workers Justice Project helped many of those workers file complaints with the agency, which then expanded the investigation using detailed pay data. The agency found DoorDash failed to pay thousands of workers at all and failed to pay thousands more on time.

The agency also found DoorDash violated the city’s Minimum Pay Rate. Although the company raised hourly pay to meet the rate in December 2023, it excluded several categories of trip time and on-call time when calculating compensable time, according to the office. The Minimum Pay Rate, which the city began enforcing in December 2023, is adjusted annually for inflation and is currently $22.13 per hour, excluding tips.

To build the case, the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection said it obtained terabytes of data from DoorDash, including billions of rows documenting how the company treated delivery workers. Its new Research and Analytics Division analyzed the data to identify more than 152 million individual payment transactions and 110 million working hours tied to the investigation.

“When a worker earns a wage, they deserve to be paid that wage – not tomorrow, not after a lawsuit, but on time and in full,” Mamdani said. “DoorDash underpaid more than 260,000 workers, and today we are getting that money back. No corporation is above the law, and this administration will keep fighting until every worker gets the pay and protections they deserve.”

Beyond the payments, the settlement sets up a worker-driven compliance monitoring program meant to catch violations as they happen. DoorDash must submit detailed data reports to the agency every month for three years. Workers Justice Project and the Workers’ Algorithm Observatory will build software that lets workers capture what DoorDash shows them about their trips and pay and share it directly with the city, and Workers Justice Project will run outreach to workers about the tool and their rights. DoorDash is barred from preventing or penalizing workers for using it. The New York Community Trust will issue grants to both organizations across the three-year monitoring period.

The settlement also requires DoorDash to make software updates so the company cannot offer a New York City worker a delivery unless that worker’s time is being recorded as compensable on-call or trip time, and to comply with the pay rule for “batched” trips, ending what the office called the unlawful practice of paying a lower rate for certain legs of a trip. DoorDash must adopt internal controls, preserve compliance records, and have an internal compliance monitor submit an annual report and sworn statement certifying compliance.

“The size of this settlement shows the damage done to workers by wage theft. But it also shows that enforcement matters,” said Deputy Mayor for Economic Justice Julie Su. “In this administration, if you steal workers’ wages, it’s not enough to just pay what you should have paid in the first place.” Department of Consumer and Worker Protection Commissioner Samuel A.A. Levine said the workers were “showing that opaque algorithms will not have the final word when it comes to how much they are paid for the hard work they do.”

The office tied the settlement to a wider enforcement push, saying the administration has secured more than $104 million in additional tips and $725 million in increased wages for delivery workers since January.

“For too long, DoorDash treated workers as disposable-stealing their wages and deactivating them, leaving families without the income they rely on,” said Ligia Guallpa, executive director of Workers’ Justice Project. “We celebrate this victory, but the fight continues: we will keep organizing for job security, safer working conditions, higher pay and respect.”

Rosendo Tacam, a delivery worker and leader of Los Deliveristas Unidos and member of Workers’ Justice Project, said he filed a complaint after DoorDash deactivated him and did not pay him for his last week of work. “I gave DoorDash everything I had, and then they deactivated me and didn’t pay me for my last week of work. I felt angry and disrespected,” Tacam said. “Today, seeing delivery workers get justice is proof that when we organize, we can make companies respect us as the essential workers we were-and continue to be-for our city.”

Council Member Sandy Nurse, who represents Bushwick, said DoorDash “thought they could shortchange their workers and get away with it. Not on our watch.” Council Member Jennifer Gutiérrez said the complex systems delivery workers navigate “doesn’t always allow these low-wage workers to seek justice for the compensation they deserve from big corporations.”

A hotline for workers with questions or who need to update their email address will open at the end of September. A second round of payments is set for early 2027 for a small group of DoorDash workers, because the company is still correcting elements of its compensable-time calculation logic that caused additional underpayments, an issue that may affect workers using DashLink. Delivery workers who believe their rights are being violated can file a complaint with the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection at nyc.gov/workers.

Featured image: Ed Reed / Mayoral Photography Office

media:content.media:description: Mayor Zohran Mamdani celebrates with a delivery worker at the Sept. 22 announcement of the city's 31.5 million settlement with DoorDash. Ed Reed / Mayoral Photography Office

item.title: Greenpointers opens vendor applications for its December 6 holiday market
item.dc:creator: Bushwick Daily News Desk
item.description: Greenpointers has opened vendor and performer applications for its free Holiday Market on December 6 at Greenpoint Loft, 67 West St, Brooklyn.
item.content:encoded:
Greenpointers has opened vendor applications for its 2026 Holiday Market, a free shopping event set for Sunday, December 6 at the Greenpoint Loft, and it is looking for makers, food vendors and performers to fill the room.

The market runs from 1 to 7 p.m. at the Greenpoint Loft, 67 West St, 5th Floor, in Brooklyn. Admission is free for visitors.

The vendor categories Greenpointers listed include ceramicists, jewelry designers, illustrators, bakers, vintage curators, clothing and accessories brands, beauty brands, food makers, artists and designers, plus, in the organizer’s words, “wonderfully weird things that don’t fit neatly into a category.” Vendors apply through an online application form. Table fees listed on the form run from $225 for a shared 4-foot table without power to $375 for an 8-foot table near an electrical outlet.

Greenpointers is also seeking DJs, musicians, artists, workshop leaders and performers to run free mini-activities during the day, listing ideas such as a holiday craft station, a portrait booth, carolers, live illustration and kids’ activities. People with a pitch can email markets@greenpointers.com.

Greenpointers, a North Brooklyn news site, has run its markets since 2012.

Featured image: Courtesy of Greenpointers

media:content.media:description: Shoppers and vendors pack the 2022 Greenpointers Holiday Market. Courtesy of Greenpointers

item.title: Mayor Mamdani plants an olive tree at Gracie Mansion with Palestinian families from Gaza
item.dc:creator: Bushwick Daily News Desk
item.description: Mayor Zohran Mamdani planted an olive tree at Gracie Mansion on Wednesday night with Palestinian families from Gaza. "May peace be our future," he wrote.
item.content:encoded:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani planted an olive tree at Gracie Mansion on Wednesday night with Palestinian families from Gaza, whom he hosted for dinner at the mayor’s official residence on the Upper East Side. “Last night I planted an olive tree at Gracie Mansion with Palestinian families from Gaza. May peace be our future,” Mamdani wrote Thursday, sharing a video of the evening.

The guests included Palestinian New Yorkers who have lost family members in Gaza and refugees who had to leave their homes, according to the Mayor’s Office. The gathering was meant to honor their contributions to the city and acknowledge the losses they have endured, the office said.

Mamdani posted the video on the day Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressed the U.N. General Assembly. In the speech, Netanyahu attacked Mamdani, calling him “the antisemitic mayor of New York.”

A few blocks south of U.N. headquarters, protesters sat in the street at First Avenue and East 39th Street to demand an end to U.S. arms to Israel and the genocide in Gaza, and 104 people were arrested. Jewish Voice for Peace, which organized the sit-in, said 400 people took part.

Three North Brooklyn officials were among those arrested: Council Member Jennifer Gutiérrez, whose district covers parts of Williamsburg, Bushwick and Ridgewood; Council Member Chi Ossé, who represents Bedford-Stuyvesant and Crown Heights; and Assembly Member Emily Gallagher, who represents Greenpoint and Williamsburg. Ossé posted a photo of himself in handcuffs with the caption “Free Palestine. Netanyahu burn in hell.”

Featured image: Image: NYC Mayor's Office video

media:content.media:description: Guests plant an olive tree on the porch of Gracie Mansion. Image: NYC Mayor's Office video

item.title: ‘Free Palestine. Netanyahu burn in hell’: Chi Ossé posts after his arrest at Netanyahu protest
item.dc:creator: Bushwick Daily News Desk
item.description: Council Members Chi Ossé and Jennifer Gutiérrez were among 104 people arrested Thursday at a Jewish Voice for Peace sit-in near the United Nations during Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's visit, according to Gutiérrez's office.
item.content:encoded:
Council Member Chi Ossé posted a photo of himself in handcuffs, surrounded by NYPD officers near the United Nations, after he was arrested Thursday at a sit-in protesting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s visit to the U.N. General Assembly. “Free Palestine. Netanyahu burn in hell,” Ossé, who represents Council District 36 in Bedford-Stuyvesant and Crown Heights, wrote in the post.

Ossé was one of 104 people arrested at the sit-in, where protesters sat in the street at First Avenue and East 39th Street, south of U.N. headquarters, to demand an end to U.S. arms to Israel and the genocide in Gaza, according to a statement from the office of Council Member Jennifer Gutiérrez. Jewish Voice for Peace organized the action and said 400 New Yorkers took part. Most participants were Jewish, and they were joined by Palestinian, Lebanese and Iranian New Yorkers, Gutiérrez’s office said.

Nine elected officials and nominees were among those arrested, according to the statement, including two more North Brooklyn officials: Gutiérrez, whose District 34 covers parts of Williamsburg, Bushwick and Ridgewood, and Assembly Member Emily Gallagher, who represents Greenpoint and Williamsburg. The others were Council Member Alexa Avilés; Aber Kawas, the Democratic nominee for State Senate; Darializa Avila Chevalier, the Democratic nominee in New York’s 13th Congressional District; and David Orkin, Christian Celeste Tate and Illapa Sairitupac, whom the office listed as Democratic nominees for State Assembly. Actor Hannah Einbinder, author Glennon Doyle and whistleblower Chelsea Manning were also arrested, the office said.

Ossé was released later Thursday. “I’m out of jail + okay,” he wrote in an Instagram story, adding, “Send Netanyahu to the Hague. Free Palestine. Free Lebanon. End the war in Iran.”

“We are safe and out of jail,” Gutiérrez wrote in her own Instagram story. “When I speak out against the genocide in Gaza, I’m speaking not only as an elected official, but as a mother who cannot accept a world where children are forced to suffer, go without food, or grow up surrounded by violence,” she said in the statement. “Every child, Palestinian or otherwise, deserves to be safe, nourished, and given the opportunity to grow up with dignity and hope.”

Gallagher posted a photo from the sit-in. “Let me say it as clearly as possible: we have a responsibility to end the genocide in Palestine,” she wrote. Bushwick Daily has asked Gallagher’s office for comment.

More than 20 city and state officials took part, according to Gutiérrez’s office. Among those it listed as present but not among the arrested were two more officials who represent parts of North Brooklyn, Council Member Sandy Nurse and State Sen. Jabari Brisport, along with Council Members Tiffany Cabán and Shahana Hanif, Assembly Member Diana Moreno and congressional nominee Brad Lander. The action was supported by groups including the Palestinian Youth Movement, NYC-DSA, the Sunrise Movement, IfNotNow and Jews for Racial and Economic Justice.

“From the streets of NYC to the halls of Congress we will be relentless in our demands to stop arming Israel,” Stefanie Fox, the executive director of Jewish Voice for Peace, said in the statement.

In his speech to the General Assembly, Netanyahu attacked New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, calling him “the antisemitic mayor of New York.”

Featured image: Photo via Chi Ossé/Instagram

media:content.media:description: Council Member Chi Ossé in police custody near the United Nations on Sept. 24, in a photo he posted to Instagram. Photo via Chi Ossé/Instagram

item.title: Friends of Greenpoint Library host annual fall book sale this weekend
item.dc:creator: Bushwick Daily News Desk
item.description: The Friends of Greenpoint Library will hold their annual Fall Book Sale at 107 Norman Ave. on Saturday, September 26 and Sunday, September 27, with proceeds supporting arts, cultural and environmental programs at the branch.
item.content:encoded:
The Friends of Greenpoint Library will hold their annual Fall Book Sale this weekend at the Greenpoint Library, 107 Norman Ave. at Leonard St., to raise money for the branch’s arts, cultural and environmental programs. The sale runs Saturday, September 26 from noon to 4 p.m. and Sunday, September 27 from 1:30 p.m. to 4 p.m.

The sale offers books for kids, teens and adults, along with a raffle featuring prizes from local businesses. Proceeds support special arts, cultural and environmental public programs at the Greenpoint Library across all ages. No book donations will be accepted on the day of the sale.

The Friends of Greenpoint Library is a group of organized volunteers who help the neighborhood branch through advocacy, fundraising and promotion. The branch, officially the Greenpoint Library and Environmental Education Center, is a 15,000-square-foot building with a gardened reading deck, a rooftop demonstration garden and separate adult, young adult and children’s reading rooms.

At the group’s fall sale in 2024, books sold for one dollar each and shoppers could enter raffles or buy a printed tote bag showing a painting of the library, made by Greenpoint artist Steve Wasterval, for twenty dollars, the Queens Ledger reported. Raffle prizes that year included a fifty-dollar gift card to The WonderMart, a two-hundred-fifty-dollar gift card to Subversive Tattoo and a one-month pass to East River Pilates, according to the Queens Ledger. That was the group’s second annual fall book sale, the Queens Ledger reported.

The Friends collect second-hand books from the community in the weeks before each sale and organize them by genre on the library’s second floor. For this year’s sale, the group accepted donations of books in new or near-new condition, with no textbooks, magazines or damaged books, Greenpointers reported.

Featured image: Brooklyn Public Library

media:content.media:description: The Greenpoint Library and Environmental Education Center at 107 Norman Ave., where the Friends of Greenpoint Library hold their Fall Book Sale on Sept. 26 and 27. Brooklyn Public Library

item.title: Free flood-resiliency comedy ‘Please Don’t Flush!’ ends NYC tour Sunday at Queens Botanical Garden
item.dc:creator: Bushwick Daily News Desk
item.description: The free flood-resiliency comedy "Please Don't Flush!" closes its multi-borough Climate Week NYC run with a final performance Sunday, September 27, at Queens Botanical Garden in Flushing.
item.content:encoded:
A free comedic stage production about flood resiliency wraps a multi-borough tour this weekend, with a final 1:30 p.m. performance Sunday, September 27, at Queens Botanical Garden in Flushing. “Please Don’t Flush!” was staged at public spaces across Queens, Brooklyn and Staten Island from September 19 to 27 as part of Climate Week NYC, and it is free to the public, QNS reported.

The play follows a community board scheduled to vote on a mysterious waterfront development that neighbors, seagulls and plumbers worry will increase inland flooding, QNS reported. The board members are derailed and instead begin planning their bi-annual gala, celebrating their second-vice-chair’s half birthday and locking the “anti-anti-anti-anti-development” coalition in the bathroom.

Sabina Sethi Unni wrote and directed the production, which features a cast of 10 actors, QNS reported. The cast includes Ray Jordan Achan, Fahad Ahmad, Amr Kotb, Amar Baines, Kshithij Hegde, Jess Balgobin, Jill Cornell, Maribelle Flint, Josabeth Simisterra and Tom Lee, who also serves as musical director. They are joined by a production team of designers, engineers, illustrators and fabricators.

Unni has been writing and directing plays on flood safety for four years, starting with her 2022 project Rainy Day Play, Queens Ledger reported. She told Queens Ledger the idea came from her day job as an organizer, through which she regularly attends community board meetings, and one “contentious, three-and-a-half hour debate about one tiny change” in particular.

“Everyone was very researched and passionate, and I was like, ‘this is a play.’ The way you watch it is very theatrical,” Unni told Queens Ledger. “But the work that organizers and council members do can sometimes feel very invisible and mundane. There’s also still a lot of silliness toward the whole institution, so it’s a great device to talk about neighborhood change and flooding.”

The production is a collaboration with the Waterfront Alliance and NYC Emergency Management, Queens Ledger reported. Jill Cornell, an NYCEM community engagement specialist who appears in the cast, told Queens Ledger she does not usually use humor in emergency preparedness work. “But working with Sabina has allowed me to widen our use of humor. And if you come and see the play, you’ll see me making fun of myself,” Cornell said.

“Flooding is a dangerous hazard, but preparedness messaging doesn’t always have to be serious for effectiveness,” Christina Farrell, commissioner of NYC Emergency Management, said in a statement carried by QNS. “‘Please Don’t Flush!’ uses humor to start important conversations about flood risk and resilience, helping New Yorkers learn how to prepare before the next storm.”

Julie Raskin, president and CEO of the Waterfront Alliance, said the production “uses the power of storytelling to make flood preparedness personal, relatable and actionable,” according to QNS. “As climate impacts become more frequent and visible, we need new ways to engage communities in preparedness and resilience,” Raskin said.

The tour earlier stopped at Staten Island Urban Center in Stapleton on September 19, Baisley Pond Park in Jamaica on September 20 and Van Alen in Gowanus on September 22, QNS reported. It is the fourth iteration of Rainy Day Plays’ public events, following performances of Flood Sensor Aunty in 2024 and 2025 that toured 12 locations across Queens, Manhattan, Brooklyn, the Bronx and Staten Island, plus one show at Wellesley College in Massachusetts.

The tour comes as the city faces heavier rainfall. In 2020, the National Climate Assessment recategorized New York City from a coastal temperate climate zone to a humid subtropical one, which, according to a 2025 statement from the City Council’s Committee on Environmental Protection, Resiliency, and Waterfronts, meant more intense storms and heavier rainfall, Queens Ledger reported. The New York State Climate Impacts Assessment projected that total precipitation in the city could increase between 4 and 11 percent, Queens Ledger reported, a projection that followed events such as Hurricane Ida, in which floods killed 13 New Yorkers.

Governor Kathy Hochul and Mayor Zohran Mamdani recently announced an $8.4 million investment to improve flood prevention infrastructure in Queens, Queens Ledger reported.

Unni told Queens Ledger her advice is to get to know your neighbors. “Whether that’s checking in on them without flood or whether you live in a basement apartment and have contacts to help you go up, not out when it does flood, it’s life-saving,” she said. “Advocacy doesn’t always help you create these relationships, but adaptive capacity and optimism can help protect your neighborhood from climate emergencies.”

Show times, locations and a form to RSVP are available at pleasedontflush.com.

Featured image: Courtesy floodsensoraunty.com

item.title: Bushwick Yacht Club and Farm to People launch a charity clothing collection for One Love Community Fridge
item.dc:creator: Bushwick Daily News Desk
item.description: Bushwick Yacht Club opens a one-week presale on a four-piece clothing collection September 24, with 100 percent of profits going to One Love Community Fridge.
item.content:encoded:
Bushwick Yacht Club is opening a one-week presale on a four-piece charity clothing collection Thursday, September 24 at 11 a.m., and 100 percent of the profits go to One Love Community Fridge, a group that runs free community fridges in Brooklyn. The Brooklyn clothing brand made the collection with local online grocer Farm to People and Brooklyn-based artist Fefi Castedo, and it will sell only through BYC’s website.

The collection is a T-shirt, a long-sleeve tee, a hoodie and a tote bag, listed on the brand’s collection page at $40 for the tote bag, $42 for the T-shirt, $55 for the long-sleeve tee and $90 for the hoodie. The presale runs one week from the 11 a.m. open. It is the third installment in BYC’s recurring charity series, an ongoing effort that pairs local artists with community partners across Bushwick.

The give-back works like this. BYC is built around a model where the money from a release goes back into the community, and for this collection all profits go directly to One Love Community Fridge. That is the group behind the community fridges that let anyone take free food, no questions asked, including one at 65 Scholes St. in East Williamsburg. One Love Community Fridge describes its mission as eradicating hunger, food insecurity and malnutrition, along with the stigma attached to all three, through work that centers access to fresh food, nutrition education and sustainability.

Castedo, a Bolivian illustrator and graphic designer based in New York, made two original designs for the collection. One is inspired by the local, New York-grown fruits and vegetables central to Farm to People’s model, and the second depicts young Brooklyn residents with local produce. The pieces carry the line “Support Local Agriculture” alongside the “Bushwick Yacht Club x Farm to People” co-brand.

“This collab, much like the brand, is about more than a T-shirt,” said Aaron Nessel, founder of Bushwick Yacht Club. “We’ve always aimed to put people over profits and this is another way to show that we care about doing the right thing. There are people that need our help and we’re lucky enough to be in a position to help them.”

Farm to People, the online farmers market delivery service based in Bushwick that connects New Yorkers to regional farmers and makers, said in the announcement that it is “excited to be part of this collaboration and support an organization that does so much to expand access to fresh, healthy food in our immediate community.” “Everyone deserves access to this kind of food, and community collaboration like this not only supports that work but celebrates it,” the company said.

Farm to People started in 2013 as a locally sourced online grocery service run out of Brooklyn, and delivers produce, local dairy, pasture-raised meats, bread and pantry staples across all five boroughs and the Tri-State area. Bushwick Yacht Club pairs its limited-edition releases with local artists and community organizations and directs the proceeds back into the community.

The presale opens September 24 at 11 a.m. Eastern and runs for one week on BYC’s collection page.

Featured image: Courtesy of Bushwick Yacht Club

media:content.media:description: The collection's tote bag and T-shirt. The four pieces go on presale Sept. 24. Courtesy of Bushwick Yacht Club

item.title: New York Games Week to bring games industry events across five boroughs October 4 to 11
item.dc:creator: Bushwick Daily News Desk
item.description: Playcrafting's New York Games Week will bring developer panels, indie showcases, pitch nights and community events across all five boroughs October 4 through 11, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
New York Games Week, a citywide games industry week organized by Playcrafting, will run October 4 through 11 with developer panels, indie showcases, business programming, pitch nights, parties and community events spread across the five boroughs, the organizers announced September 21. Details are posted at nygamesweek.com.

The week gathers developer panels, indie showcases, business-to-business programming, pitch nights, parties and community events at venues across all five boroughs, organized by a team of game industry professionals, according to co-founder Krysti Pryde.

Pryde said the goal is to uplift the current game developer community while turning New York City into a destination on the global games industry calendar, and to make the city a place people want to live and make games. She described the format as “London Games Week meets New York Tech Week.”

The event is backed by the Mayor’s Office of Media and Entertainment and NYCEDC, Pryde said. Confirmed partners include the NYU Game Center, the Fashion in Gaming Awards, Game-a-Palooza, Game Design Future Lab, New York Comic Con, SEGA and Latinx In Gaming, with more partner announcements to come, according to the organizers.

Pryde said the team is still building out programming as the week approaches. Individual event listings are posted at nygamesweek.com.

Featured image: Courtesy nygamesweek.com

media:content.media:description: New York Games Week logo, file photo Courtesy nygamesweek.com
